title: Generating Functions Lab
summary: Generating functions as a calculus for discrete structures: problem, discrete object, encode, manipulate, read coefficient, answer, verify.

conventions.egf: A(x) = Σ aₙxⁿ/n!; strips show the counts aₙ
conventions.dft: Â_k = A(ω^k) with ω = e^{2πi/N}; aₙ = (1/N) Σ_k A(ω^k) ω^{−kn}. numpy.fft uses e^{−2πi/N}, so its entry k is entry N − k here.
conventions.fibonacci: F₀ = 0, F₁ = 1; the strip 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 is aₙ = Fₙ₊₁
conventions.exactness: Counting uses exact integers and rationals; roots-of-unity values are exact in ℤ[ζ_N]; floating point only for pictures and asymptotics, with stated tolerances.

levels.title: What is a generating function?
levels.when_to_use: Use an encoding whenever you want to treat a whole sequence as one algebraic object.
levels.key: A generating function is an encoding of coefficients, not primarily a function to plug numbers into.

levels.title: Geometric series
levels.when_to_use: Use the geometric series whenever an object is any number of copies of one thing.
levels.key: The formal identity 1 + x + x² + ⋯ = 1/(1 − x) needs no convergence; |x| < 1 matters only in the analytic view.

levels.title: Shifts
levels.when_to_use: Use a shift when a sequence is the same as another one, delayed by a fixed amount.
levels.key: Multiplying by x^k slides the coefficient strip k places right: [xⁿ] x^k A(x) = aₙ₋ₖ.

levels.title: Addition and subtraction
levels.when_to_use: Use addition when objects split into disjoint types, and subtraction to discard a class of forbidden objects.
levels.key: Disjoint union adds generating functions; removing a subclass subtracts its generating function.

levels.title: Differentiation
levels.when_to_use: Use differentiation when coefficients must be weighted by n, as in marking one atom or computing a mean.
levels.key: d/dx multiplies aₙ by n and shifts left; x·d/dx multiplies by n in place: Σ n xⁿ = x/(1 − x)².

levels.title: Solving a recurrence (Fibonacci)
levels.when_to_use: Use recurrence solving when a sequence is specified recursively by finitely many shifted terms.
levels.key: Shifted copies of the recurrence become xF(x) and x²F(x); the recurrence becomes a linear equation for F(x).

levels.title: Partial fractions and Binet's formula
levels.when_to_use: Use partial fractions when a rational generating function factors into simple poles.
levels.key: Partial fractions turn a complicated rational generating function into a sum of simple coefficient machines.

levels.title: Cauchy product and convolution
levels.when_to_use: Use a product when an object decomposes into independently chosen pieces whose sizes add.
levels.key: A product of generating functions is the convolution of coefficients: cₙ = Σ aₖbₙ₋ₖ, a diagonal of the product grid.

levels.title: Coin change
levels.when_to_use: Use a product of geometric series when each kind of part may be used any number of times independently.
levels.key: Each denomination contributes an independent factor 1/(1 − x^d); [xⁿ] of the product counts the solutions of a + 2b + 5c = n.

levels.title: Restricted compositions
levels.when_to_use: Use the sequence construction when an object is an ordered list of parts from a fixed class.
levels.key: A sequence of parts from P(x) is 1 + P + P² + ⋯ = 1/(1 − P(x)).

levels.title: Symbolic combinatorics
levels.when_to_use: Use the symbolic method when you can describe the objects by a grammar of sums, products and sequences.
levels.key: CHOICE is A + B, PAIR is AB (convolution), SEQUENCE is 1/(1 − A): the construction is the equation.

levels.title: Composition (substitution)
levels.when_to_use: Use composition when atoms of one structure are replaced by structures of another kind.
levels.key: Product combines independent sizes; composition replaces each atom by a whole structure: A(B(x)).

levels.title: Catalan numbers
levels.when_to_use: Use an implicit equation when the class is defined recursively in terms of itself.
levels.key: C = 1 + xC² is a quadratic; its power-series root (1 − √(1 − 4x))/(2x) gives Cₙ = C(2n, n)/(n + 1).

levels.title: Lagrange inversion
levels.when_to_use: Use Lagrange inversion when the generating function is defined implicitly by T = xφ(T).
levels.key: [xⁿ]Tᵏ = (k/n)[uⁿ⁻ᵏ]φ(u)ⁿ: a coefficient of an unknown series becomes a coefficient of a known power.

levels.title: Exponential generating functions
levels.when_to_use: Use an EGF when objects carry distinct labels and decompositions require choosing subsets of those labels.
levels.key: A(x) = Σ aₙxⁿ/n!: dividing by n! removes the ambient permutation factor of the labels.

levels.title: The labelled product
levels.when_to_use: Use the labelled product when a labelled object splits into two labelled pieces whose label sets partition the labels.
levels.key: cₙ = Σ C(n, k) aₖbₙ₋ₖ: the binomial coefficient is the act of choosing which labels go left; EGFs multiply.

levels.title: The exponential formula
levels.when_to_use: Use the exponential formula when every object is an unordered set of labelled connected components.
levels.key: A(x) = exp(C(x)) = 1 + C + C²/2! + C³/3! + ⋯: k components form a k-fold labelled product, divided by k! because they are unordered.

levels.title: Permutations and cycles
levels.when_to_use: Use PERM = SET(CYC) when you need permutations by cycle structure.
levels.key: PERMUTATION = SET(CYCLE): exp(log 1/(1 − x)) = 1/(1 − x), so n! permutations; marking cycles gives Stirling numbers.

levels.title: Bivariate generating functions
levels.when_to_use: Use a bivariate generating function when you want a second parameter (marked by y) alongside size.
levels.key: Setting y = 1 marginalises; ∂/∂y at y = 1 sums the marked parameter, giving its mean Hₙ.

levels.title: Probability generating functions
levels.when_to_use: Use a probability generating function for sums of independent integer-valued random variables.
levels.key: G_{X+Y}(z) = G_X(z)G_Y(z): counting convolution = probability convolution = polynomial multiplication.

levels.title: Roots-of-unity filters
levels.when_to_use: Use a roots-of-unity filter when only coefficients in selected congruence classes matter.
levels.key: (1/m)Σⱼ ω^{j(n−r)} is 1 when n ≡ r (mod m) and 0 otherwise: the phasors of unwanted classes cancel.

levels.title: Finite generating functions as vectors
levels.when_to_use: Use the evaluation representation when a finite coefficient vector is easier to manipulate through its values.
levels.key: The DFT is the change of coordinates from the coefficients of a polynomial to its values at the roots of unity.

levels.title: The DFT matrix
levels.when_to_use: Use the DFT when a finite coefficient vector is easier to manipulate through polynomial values at roots of unity.
levels.key: Row k of the DFT matrix is (1, ωᵏ, ω²ᵏ, …): evaluating A at ωᵏ is a dot product. A(1) = 10, A(i) = −2 − 2i, A(−1) = −2, A(−i) = −2 + 2i.

levels.title: Inverse DFT as coefficient extraction
levels.when_to_use: Use the inverse DFT to read coefficients back from values at the roots of unity.
levels.key: aₙ = (1/N)Σₖ A(ωᵏ)ω^{−kn}: a finite coefficient-extraction formula, and the same phenomenon as the roots-of-unity filter.

levels.title: The cyclic convolution theorem
levels.when_to_use: Use the convolution theorem when a cyclic convolution is cheaper as pointwise multiplication of DFTs.
levels.key: DFT(a ⊛ b) = DFT(a)·DFT(b): multiplication modulo xᴺ − 1 becomes coordinatewise multiplication.

levels.title: Polynomial multiplication and the FFT
levels.when_to_use: Use the FFT viewpoint when multiplying long polynomials or convolving long sequences.
levels.key: A(x) = A_even(x²) + xA_odd(x²) halves the work at each level: O(n log n) instead of O(n²).

levels.title: Rational GFs and automata
levels.when_to_use: Use a transfer matrix when objects are words accepted by a finite automaton.
levels.key: v_{n+1} = Mvₙ gives Σ vₙxⁿ = (I − xM)⁻¹v₀: finite-state constraints give rational generating functions.

levels.title: Partitions and q-series
levels.when_to_use: Use an infinite product when each part size can be chosen independently any number of times.
levels.key: Each part size k contributes 1 + xᵏ + x²ᵏ + ⋯; the product over all k is Π 1/(1 − xᵏ).

levels.title: Euler's partition identity
levels.when_to_use: Use an equality of generating functions to prove that two families are equinumerous.
levels.key: Π(1 + xᵏ) = Π(1 − x²ᵏ)/(1 − xᵏ) = Π 1/(1 − x²ᵏ⁻¹): an algebraic identity, also explained by a bijection.

levels.title: Singularities and growth
levels.when_to_use: Use singularity analysis when exact formulas matter less than the growth of coefficients.
levels.key: The nearest singularity sets the exponential growth: a pole at ρ gives coefficients ≈ ρ⁻ⁿ.

levels.title: Singularity analysis
levels.when_to_use: Use singularity analysis when the generating function has an algebraic singularity on its circle of convergence.
levels.key: Location of the singularity → exponential factor (4ⁿ); its type (square root) → polynomial correction (n^{−3/2}).

levels.title: Saddle-point intuition
levels.when_to_use: Use the saddle-point view when the generating function is entire or has no useful singularity.
levels.key: Choosing r at the saddle (r ≈ n) concentrates the integral near z = r and recovers Stirling: 1/n! ≈ eⁿ/(nⁿ√(2πn)).

levels.title: Multivariate generating functions
levels.when_to_use: Use multivariate generating functions when objects carry several sizes at once.
levels.key: 1/(1 − x − y) has a_{m,n} = C(m+n, m); the diagonal [xⁿyⁿ] = C(2n, n) is selected geometrically and has GF 1/√(1 − 4t).

levels.title: The unifying picture
levels.when_to_use: Use this map to pick a representation before picking a trick.
levels.key: Generating functions are changes of representation; at roots of unity, convolution becomes multiplication.

spec_corrections: Spec §2 and Level 2 call 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 'Fibonacci(n)'; with F₀ = 0 (as Level 5 uses) that strip is aₙ = Fₙ₊₁, so the lab labels it that way.
Spec §16 uses ω = i for N = 4, i.e. ω = e^{+2πi/N}; the lab keeps that sign and notes that numpy's fft (e^{−2πi/N}) lists A(−i) = −2 + 2i where the lab lists A(i) = −2 − 2i.
Spec §12's example '21' is [x⁷] of 1/(1 − x − x²) (compositions of 7 into 1s and 2s); the symbolic-method lesson opens on exactly that case.
